---
title: "Quiz: phase correlation"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Phase correlation divides every $A_k\overline{B_k}$ by its size and takes the inverse FFT.

---

**Q1.** Why does the cross-correlation of two micrographs usually have a broad peak?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which waves are strongest in a typical image, and how fast does their vote change with the shift?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Most of an image's strength is in the slow waves (smooth brightness changes). Their votes are the largest, and a slow wave still agrees at shifts a few pixels away from the true one. The sum is a wide hill rather than a spike.
:::

---

**Q2.** Which property of the Fourier transform makes phase correlation work?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does a shift do to the sizes and to the phases of the waves?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The shift theorem: shifting an image multiplies each $F_k$ by a phase factor $e^{-2\pi i k t/N}$; the sizes $|F_k|$ do not change. All the information about the shift is in the phase differences, so the sizes can be thrown away.
:::

---

**Q3.** Image B is a perfect circular shift of A by $t_0$. What does the phase-correlation surface look like?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
After normalising, every frequency is a pure phase ramp.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A single spike of height 1 at $t_0$ and zero everywhere else: the inverse DFT of $e^{-2\pi i kt_0/N}$ for all $k$ is a delta.
:::

---

**Q4.** B is A with twice the contrast and 50 grey levels brighter. How does the phase-correlation surface change? And the cross-correlation?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Which $B_k$ does the offset change, and what does the gain do to the phases?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Phase correlation: not at all. The gain multiplies every $B_k$ by 2 (same phase), the offset only changes $B_0$, and after normalisation $R_0$ has size 1 whatever $B_0$ is. Cross-correlation: the surface doubles (gain) and the mean term changes (offset); with the means subtracted, only the factor 2 remains, but an uneven brightness change would move CC's peak.
:::

---

**Q5.** Why does phase correlation suffer more from noise than cross-correlation?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Where in the spectrum is the noise as strong as the signal?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At high frequencies the image signal is weak and the noise is about as strong: the phase differences there are random. Cross-correlation gives these frequencies small votes (they are weak); phase correlation gives them the same vote as the strong low frequencies. Many random votes make a noisy floor that can be higher than the spike.
:::

---

**Q6.** Name two ways to make phase correlation more robust to noise.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Change the weights of the frequencies.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Multiply the normalised spectrum by a **low-pass** weight that fades out the highest frequencies; or normalise only **partly**, dividing by $|A_k\overline{B_k}|^p$ with $0 < p < 1$, which keeps some of the strength information. (Also: an $\varepsilon$ in the denominator, averaging or smoothing the images first.)
:::

---

**Q7.** Without a taper, phase correlation of two crops often shows a false peak at shift $(0, 0)$ and a bright cross in the spectrum. Why?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What does the DFT assume happens at the border of a crop?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The DFT treats each crop as periodic, so the left border meets the right one (and top meets bottom), usually with a jump in brightness. These jump lines produce strong waves along the axes (the cross) and they are at the same place in both crops: they do not move with the shift, so they vote for zero shift. A Hann taper brings both crops smoothly to zero at the border and removes the jumps.
:::

---

**Q8.** Two tiles give a phase-correlation peak of 0.08 and a peak ratio of 1.05. What do you conclude?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What do the height and the ratio measure?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Do not trust this shift. A ratio of 1.05 means the second-best shift is almost as good; a height of 0.08 means very little shared content (or a lot of noise). Typical reasons: a nearly empty tile, a periodic texture, a very small overlap. A mosaic program should drop this pair or give it a small weight.
:::
